questions.question: Oliver, you said something in our pre-chat that I haven't been able to shake — that Oliphant makes Edward's voice *more* entertaining to read aloud than Hester's moral clarity, and she knows exactly what she's doing. Can you actually demonstrate that? Read us something from Edward's speeches and tell us what you're hearing in the rhythm.
questions.intent: Get Oliver to perform c15:p41 and articulate the seduction-of-the-reader argument — sets up the core debate about whether Edward is villain or something more disturbing

questions.question: Edmund, you'd push back on that, wouldn't you? Because you told me Edward's 'the weak will always go to the wall' line is a confession of moral failure — cowardice dressed as philosophy, you said. But if Oliver's right and that speech is genuinely magnetic, does that change your reading? Is Edward a coward, or is he something we find ourselves enjoying a little too much?
questions.intent: Force Edmund to reckon with Oliver's entertainment argument — draws out the tension between Edmund's character-morality reading and Oliver's craft-and-complicity reading

questions.question: Daniel, I want to bring you in here because you're going to land this somewhere completely different — you told me Edward isn't really a villain or even a coward, he's just the *system speaking plainly*. But if that's true, does Oliver's point actually help your argument? Like, isn't it more unsettling that the system is *charming*?
questions.intent: Get Daniel to engage with the entertainment argument on his own structural terms — creates a three-way friction between individual moral failure, narrative seduction, and systemic critique

questions.question: Edmund, let's go to Hester's walk — c15:p23, that passage about her being 'a whole retinue, a body-guard to herself.' You read that as Oliphant's eye for the body betraying inner conflict. Daniel reads it as surveillance — every movement she makes gets read as proof she needs protecting. Those feel like fundamentally different novels. Which one is Oliphant actually writing?
questions.intent: Directly stage the Edmund vs. Daniel disagreement — individual conscience versus structural trap — using a specific shared passage both want to quote

questions.question: Final thing for this segment — we've been circling Catherine. Oliver, you mentioned that the 'reverse of the medal' image in c35:p92 is *narrative mechanics*, not psychology — Oliphant showing us how stories flip. Daniel thinks it's Catherine finally seeing her own complicity. Edmund thinks it's the slow dissolution of comfortable illusion. Is there actually a right answer here, or is that ambiguity the whole point of the opening move Oliphant is making?
questions.intent: Bring Catherine into the conversation as the segment's closing question — surfaces the three-way disagreement about whether the novel is about craft, conscience, or complicity, and lets the experts argue about what the house actually *is*

briefs.steering_notes: This segment should feel like it's building toward one genuinely unresolved question: is Oliphant writing a novel about individual moral character, or about how systems disguise themselves as human nature? Don't let anyone win that argument cleanly. Oliver's entertainment thesis is the wild card — keep returning to it because it unsettles both Edmund's moral seriousness and Daniel's structural critique. Push for readings aloud where possible; the prose will do work the panelists can't anticipate. Watch for Edmund and Daniel talking past each other on the walk passage — that's where the real friction is and it's worth slowing down for.
cross_engagement_targets: Oliver's claim that Edward's voice is more entertaining than Hester's moral clarity directly challenges Edmund's reading of Edward as simply a moral failure — Edmund needs to account for the seduction, not just the cowardice
Daniel's surveillance reading of the walk passage (c15:p23) and Edmund's inner-conflict reading use the *same* quoted text to argue for opposite things — stage this collision explicitly

Daniel's insistence that Catherine's arc is about complicity rather than betrayal directly contradicts Edmund's framing of her suffering as real and earned — this should surface when Catherine comes up

Oliver's point that c35:p92 is narrative mechanics rather than psychology pushes back on both Edmund (who reads it as moral dissolution) and Daniel (who reads it politically) — all three have staked a claim on this image

questions.question: Oliver, you've talked about how certain passages in this novel only really come alive when they're read aloud — so let's start there. Can you take us to that vertigo passage, c9:p82, and read it for us? And then tell me: what does a voice have to *do* with those lines that a silent reader just can't get?
questions.intent: Open with a performance moment to hook the audience, let Oliver demonstrate his strongest claim about voice and embodiment, and prime Daniel and Edmund to contest what the reading implies about what the passage *means*

questions.question: Daniel, Oliver just gave us Hester's vertigo as something almost beautiful — grief and recognition, the body learning. But you called it claustrophobia. You said she's feeling the walls of her economic cage. Those are very different women we're watching. Which one is Oliphant actually writing?
questions.intent: Force the central disagreement between Oliver and Daniel into the open — romantic-sublime Hester versus structurally-trapped Hester — and get Daniel to his strongest materialist reading

questions.question: Edmund, you've argued that calling this a story about thwarted ambitions is actually an anachronism — that Hester isn't after a career or public recognition, she's after something older and more serious: family honour, moral coherence. But then how do you deal with Hester's own line at c9:p32 — 'You speak of ladies only. Where was my father?' That sounds less like a woman defending honour and more like a woman who's furious and asking a very pointed question. What do you do with the steel in that line?
questions.intent: Push Edmund off his 'moral coming-of-age' reading by weaponising the passage he's least comfortable with — get him to either accommodate the feminist reading or sharpen his disagreement with it

questions.question: Daniel, you said the most marginalised figure in this whole novel isn't Hester at all — it's her mother, the woman whose twenty pounds gets extracted and called devotion. Can you read us that passage, c9:p28, and make the case? Because Edmund hears the same lines and finds them genuinely moving. Oliver finds them the emotional hinge of the whole sequence. You seem to be saying: yes, moving, and that's exactly the problem. Is the novel complicit in what it's describing?
questions.intent: Get Daniel to his sharpest and most provocative claim — that the novel is ideologically captured by what it's anatomising — and set Edmund up to defend Oliphant's moral seriousness against a Marxist reading

questions.question: Edmund, you said that what Hester faces at the end of this sequence is a genuine tragic dilemma — she has knowledge she can't unknow and probably can't speak. But Oliver says that's a *performance* problem, not a moral one: the silence works because it's suspense, it's Oliphant playing her audience. And Daniel says the silence is structural — women are made silent, it's not a free choice. Who's right? Or is there a version where all three of you are describing the same silence from different angles?
questions.intent: Synthesise the three competing readings by forcing the experts to locate themselves relative to each other — create a moment of genuine intellectual triangulation rather than parallel monologue, and see if productive agreement or sharpened disagreement emerges

briefs.steering_notes: The energy in this segment should feel like three people who've all read the same book and arrived at completely different novels. Let Oliver perform first — it warms the room and gives Daniel and Edmund something concrete to agree or disagree with. The key fault line is: is Hester's suffering a structural symptom, a moral education, or a performance of felt experience? Don't let anyone get away with 'all three' without making them earn it. Push for specificity: which passage, which word, which choice by Oliphant. If Daniel and Edmund are talking past each other, bring Oliver in as a kind of mediator-through-performance — ask him to read the contested passage and let the reading itself be the argument.
cross_engagement_targets: Oliver reads c9:p82 and frames it as earned grief — Daniel should immediately contest whether 'earned' is even the right category when the emotion is produced by systemic confinement rather than personal failure

Edmund defends the twenty-pounds passage as morally serious and moving — Daniel's pre-interview response directly contradicts this: he says that being moved is the mechanism of extraction, not a counter to it. This is the sharpest direct clash in the segment.

Oliver argues the silences are suspense and craft — Edmund argues they're moral communication — Daniel argues they're ideological cover. All three are talking about the same technical device with completely different ontologies underneath. Surface this explicitly.

Edmund's claim that 'thwarted ambitions' is an anachronism collides directly with Daniel's structural reading — Edmund thinks Daniel is projecting modern grievance onto a Victorian text; Daniel thinks Edmund is aestheticising oppression. Let this run.

briefs.segment_name: The Weight of Class and Capital

questions.question: Daniel, you've argued that Catherine's hatred of Hester isn't personal—it's structural. She inherited a catastrophe she didn't make and spent her life managing it. But Edmund would say that's letting Catherine off the hook, that her vindictiveness is a choice, a moral failure that belongs to her. So which is it—is Catherine a victim of capital or is she cruel?
questions.intent: Force the sharpest possible confrontation between Daniel's structural reading and Edmund's moral realism reading, using Catherine as the battleground

questions.question: Oliver, you made me genuinely excited about this in our pre-conversation—you said Oliphant is essentially a music hall writer pretending to be a domestic realist. Can you read us that John Vernon line—'Catherine's growing an old maid, she must look alive'—and then explain what you mean by that? Because Daniel hears pure structural violence in that line, and I want to know if you're hearing something completely different.
questions.intent: Get Oliver to perform the line aloud, then contrast his comedic-formal reading with Daniel's ideological reading of the same passage (c1:p26)

questions.question: Edmund, you want to read the Lawrence portrait passage—Mrs. John Vernon posed like a painting, all beauty and no agency—as Oliphant being *ironic*, laughing at her self-theatricalization. But Daniel says that beauty and refinement are exactly what makes oppression look like grace, that it's the system aestheticizing its own cruelty. Who's right about what Oliphant is doing there?
questions.intent: Trigger the three-way disagreement about c1:p90—irony versus complicity versus aestheticization—and get Edmund to defend his anti-structural reading against the strongest version of the structural argument

questions.question: Oliver, you said you want to *perform* that passage about Hester's half-knowledge—the torture of imagination supplementing what she's not allowed to know. Will you do it? And then tell me: is the sentence structure itself doing political work, or is that a category error—are we just describing good prose?
questions.intent: Get Oliver to read c34:p114 aloud and then force the question of whether his formal claim about syntax encoding privilege is genuinely distinct from Daniel's ideological argument or secretly the same thing

questions.question: Edmund, your strongest claim is that Oliphant shows powerlessness as a *temptation* toward moral failure—not an excuse for it. But here's my problem: Hester is young, broke, dependent, and kept in deliberate ignorance. At what point does the weight of that constraint actually become morally relevant? Or does Oliphant just not care?
questions.intent: Push Edmund to the limit of his moral realism argument and see whether he concedes any ground to structural factors—this should draw Daniel back in hard

briefs.steering_notes: The central tension is Edmund's moral realism versus Daniel's structural/economic reading, with Oliver's formal-aesthetic argument cutting across both. Keep returning the conversation to specific passages rather than letting it stay abstract—the three panelists actually agree on *which* passages matter but disagree sharply on what they mean, which is ideal. If Daniel and Edmund start talking past each other, use Oliver as a wedge: his claim that the prose *performs* constraint is neither pure moralism nor pure ideology and can reframe the argument. Watch for the moment where someone concedes partial ground—that's when the conversation gets genuinely interesting. Don't let Edmund's 'moral realism' label go unchallenged; it's doing a lot of work and Daniel will want to name it as a form of victim-blaming.
cross_engagement_targets: Daniel's reading of Catherine as structural victim directly contradicts Edmund's claim that Catherine's vindictiveness originates in her own will—this is the sharpest disagreement in the segment and should be made explicit early

Oliver and Daniel nominally agree that Edward's assumption of Hester's love encodes class privilege, but Oliver frames this as a formal/syntactic phenomenon while Daniel frames it as foundational to the economic system—pressing both on whether that distinction matters will generate productive friction

Edmund reads the Lawrence portrait as Oliphant's ironic commentary on Mrs. Vernon's self-theatricalization; Daniel reads the same passage as the system aestheticizing oppression; Oliver reads it as the comedy of the gap between beauty and powerlessness—all three readings of c1:p90 are incompatible and should be staged as a direct three-way confrontation

Both Edmund and Oliver want to quote the Hester half-knowledge passage (c34:p114) but for completely different reasons—Edmund to show Oliphant naming feminine suffering without sentimentality or structural excuse, Oliver to demonstrate how prose syntax itself performs gendered constraint. Getting both to engage the same passage will surface whether their disagreement is about form, politics, or both

briefs.segment_name: Narrative Games: Oliphant's Technique of Revelation

questions.question: Oliver, you said before we started recording that Oliphant is basically *directing* actors in these passages—that the prose is theatrical instruction. Can you show us what you mean with that passage from chapter 37, where Hester's face drains of colour? Because I want to know: is that a novelist at work, or is it something stranger?
questions.intent: Get Oliver to read c37:p105 aloud and make the case for Oliphant as performance artist, setting up Edmund's pushback about conscience and Daniel's about whose interiority gets this treatment

questions.question: Edmund, you called what Oliphant is doing in these passages 'confessional'—you said she positions the reader as priest. But Oliver's just shown us something that sounds more like theatre than confession booth. How do you square that? Is Hester performing guilt, or *feeling* it?
questions.intent: Force the theological vs theatrical disagreement into the open—Edmund's reading of moral opacity versus Oliver's reading of performed sensation

questions.question: Daniel, both Oliver and Edmund are giving us readings where Hester's interiority is the *point*—whether it's felt in the body or examined by the soul. But you told me before we started that the technique is actually hiding something. What is it hiding, and can you show us in that chapter 43 passage—'as if it had been in a book'—where you see the sleight of hand happening?
questions.intent: Get Daniel to read c43:p89 and make the ideological-evasion argument, directly challenging both Edmund's 'phenomenology of shock' and Oliver's 'narrative wink'

questions.question: Let me put Catherine's death to you directly, Edmund—chapter 45, the 'supernatural chill,' the ivory face against the dark curtains. Oliver thinks Oliphant is making our skin crawl on purpose, Daniel thinks she's aestheticizing what is actually institutional abandonment. You think it's about ordinary catastrophe and moral knowledge. Who's closest to what's actually on the page?
questions.intent: Three-way collision on c45:p30—force all three readings into direct comparison on a single passage and let the disagreement escalate

questions.question: Oliver, you made me laugh before we started when you said Oliphant has a 'wicked sense of the ridiculous'—and Edmund and Daniel both looked slightly alarmed. Is there actually comedy in these passages? Because Daniel's reading sounds like tragedy all the way down, and Edmund's sounds like a sermon. Where's the joke?
questions.intent: Use Oliver's point about c19:p80 and Oliphant's comic sensibility to lighten the register and expose whether Edmund and Daniel's frameworks can accommodate Oliphant's irony and self-aware narrative winking

briefs.steering_notes: The real tension in this segment is a three-way fight about what Oliphant's technique is *for*—Oliver says performance and intimacy, Edmund says moral examination and conscience, Daniel says ideological mystification. Don't let any one frame dominate too early. The best radio comes from keeping all three in play simultaneously, especially on the shared passages (c37:p105 and c43:p89 are quoted by all three experts—use that overlap as a pressure point). Push for actual quotation: Oliver especially will read aloud if invited. Watch for the moment when Edmund and Daniel, despite their differences, are both uncomfortable with Oliver's aestheticism—that's a useful alliance to surface and then destabilize. The comedy question at the end is a release valve but also a genuine test of each framework's flexibility.
cross_engagement_targets: All three experts quote c37:p105 but for entirely different reasons—Oliver for theatrical direction, Edmund for permanent moral opacity, Daniel for fractured class consciousness. Ask them to respond directly to each other's readings of the same sentence.

Edmund's claim that c43:p89 shows 'the phenomenology of shock' directly contradicts Daniel's reading of it as ideological estrangement—this is the sharpest disagreement in the segment and should be forced into explicit confrontation.

Daniel's argument that Catherine's death is 'death by neglect aestheticized as mystery' is a direct challenge to Edmund's 'ordinary catastrophe' reading and Oliver's 'uncanny' reading—all three need to be in the room together on c45:p30.

Oliver's insistence on Oliphant's comedy and self-awareness (the narrative wink in c43:p89) is incompatible with Edmund's serious theological frame—Edmund's pre-interview said 'she is not playing games; she is saving souls.' Surface this directly.

briefs.segment_name: Edward's Reckoning: Speculation, Flight, and Return

questions.question: Edmund, you've described Edward's situation as a *chosen* captivity — he could walk away from Catherine but won't. But when Oliphant writes 'too sincere and real to be capable of his usual self-suppression,' isn't she giving him something more than weakness? Doesn't she suggest he's being crushed by something that has genuine weight?
questions.intent: Get Edmund to defend his moral-culpability reading in its strongest form, setting up the collision with Oliver's sympathy reading and Daniel's structural reading

questions.question: Oliver, you want to read the artillery simile — 'a battery of artillery planted in front of this peaceful Grange with all its matches alight' — as *performing* violence in the syntax itself. Can you actually read us that passage and show us what you mean? Because Edmund thinks it's about Edward's soul and Daniel thinks it's about capitalism, and I want to hear what you think is happening at the sentence level.
questions.intent: Get Oliver to read the passage aloud and demonstrate his close-reading argument, which will force the others to respond to specific words rather than abstractions

questions.question: Daniel, you called the brandy-and-laudanum line 'the smoking gun' — that Oliphant sees speculation as anesthesia for the powerless, not as greed. But Edmund would say that framing is exactly the trap Oliphant is *exposing* — that Edward tells himself that story. So whose side is the novel actually on when it uses that comparison?
questions.intent: Force a direct confrontation between Daniel's systemic reading and Edmund's moral reading, both using the same passage as evidence

questions.question: Edmund, help me with the word 'unconscious' — 'Catherine, the unconscious cause of his imprisonment.' You say that makes Edward's rage more morally damning. But Daniel would say it makes *Catherine* more damning, as an instrument of a system she can't even see. Who is Oliphant actually indicting there?
questions.intent: Triangulate the Catherine question across all three experts — Edmund sees Edward's culpability, Daniel sees structural complicity, Oliver sees mutual dignity in suffering — and let them fight over a single word

questions.question: Oliver, you've argued these papers are essentially a MacGuffin — that Edward could as easily have reached for gambling or seduction. But Daniel thinks the *specific* thing being speculation is the whole point, capitalism's seductive logic and all that. So does it matter that it's financial papers and not a deck of cards?
questions.intent: Produce the sharpest possible disagreement between Oliver and Daniel, forcing both to commit to whether the novel's subject is psychology or political economy

briefs.steering_notes: This segment has a genuine three-way disagreement with real stakes: moral culpability (Edmund) vs. psychological sympathy (Oliver) vs. structural critique (Daniel). The temptation will be to let them talk past each other using the same passages as proof-texts for incompatible readings — that's actually the feature, not the bug. Push them to name the *same line* and fight over it. The artillery metaphor and the laudanum comparison are the two live wires; return to them whenever the conversation gets abstract. Don't let anyone escape into general claims about Victorian fiction — bring them back to the sentences. The most productive moment will be when Edmund and Daniel are forced to agree that the novel is doing something Oliphant herself may not fully endorse — the tension between judgment and understanding Oliver names.
cross_engagement_targets: Oliver says Edward's resentment is 'pathetic but dignified' — Edmund says that dignity is precisely Edward's self-delusion. Ask Oliver to respond directly to Edmund's 'chosen chains' framing.

Daniel and Edmund are both using the 'unconscious cause' line but as evidence for opposite arguments — Catherine as systemic mechanism (Daniel) vs. Catherine as moral mirror (Edmund). Surface this directly.

Oliver claims the papers are a MacGuffin; Daniel says the papers being financial speculation is load-bearing. This is a binary disagreement that can produce a clean radio moment if the host just names it plainly and steps back.

Edmund insists the novel has 'moral clarity' about Edward's culpability; Daniel insists the novel's radicalism lies in its tension between judgment and understanding. Oliver agrees with Daniel on this. Two-against-one moments are good radio — let it happen.

briefs.segment_name: Loneliness and Authority: Catherine Vernon's Paradox

questions.question: Oliver, you used a word that's been stuck in my head—you said Catherine is 'cruel.' Not tragic, not sympathetic, but genuinely cruel. And you've got this quote you want to read where Oliphant uses the word 'blow'—where Catherine laughs and flinches at the same moment. Can you take us to that passage and make the case that we shouldn't let Catherine off the hook?
questions.intent: Establish the cruelty reading up front and get Trevelyan to perform the 'blow' quote, which will immediately provoke Leigh and Rosen

questions.question: Edmund, I can hear you wanting to jump in already. Because your pre-interview basically said the opposite—that Catherine is the novel's moral centre, that she's earned her authority through sacrifice. So is Oliver being too hard on her, or is he just describing what moral seriousness actually looks like from the outside when it has power behind it?
questions.intent: Force the direct confrontation between 'cruelty' and 'moral centre' readings—get Leigh to defend Catherine without sounding like he's excusing her

questions.question: Daniel, you've got a different kind of problem with both of these takes, haven't you? Because whether Catherine is a cruel tyrant or a tragic moral authority, both readings are still basically about Catherine as an individual. And you want to say—the loneliness isn't personal, it's structural. She's not lonely because of who she is, she's lonely because of what the system needs her to be. Can you make that case?
questions.intent: Bring in the structural/systemic argument as a counterweight to both character-based readings, set up the 'necessary woman' thesis

questions.question: Edmund, let's go to the scene at c16:p62—the veil passage, Captain Morgan jumping up with his rheumatism. You read Morgan's interruption as a moral summons, a conscience arriving at exactly the right moment. Oliver thinks it's a music-hall pratfall. Daniel thinks it's the patriarchy literally inserting itself into a woman's emotional life through an old man's body. Can you read us that passage and then tell me why you're right and they're both wrong?
questions.intent: Get the veil passage read aloud, then use the three competing interpretations of a single scene to generate genuine triangulated argument

questions.question: Dan, you said something in our pre-interview that I haven't been able to shake—that Hester won't replace Catherine, she'll *become* her. Which is a kind of horror story ending for the whole novel. Does Oliphant know she's writing that? And if she does, what does that say about whether any of the rebellion in this book—Hester's, Mrs. John's fantasies, even the romantic connection with Roland—actually means anything at all?
questions.intent: End the segment on the darkest possible note—Hester as Catherine's heir, rebellion as reproduction of the system—and invite Trevelyan and Leigh to either rescue some hope or agree it's a tragedy

briefs.steering_notes: The segment has a natural three-way tension that should be kept alive: Trevelyan reads comedy and cruelty, Leigh reads moral architecture and earned authority, Rosen reads structural entrapment. Don't let any two of them gang up on the third for too long—the most interesting moments will be when Leigh and Rosen agree that Trevelyan is being too comic, or when Trevelyan and Rosen agree that Leigh is too forgiving of Catherine, then immediately disagree about why. Push toward the veil passage as the central exhibit—all three have something to say about it and they're genuinely incompatible readings. Save the 'Hester becomes Catherine' thesis for the end; it reframes everything and should land with weight.
cross_engagement_targets: Trevelyan's 'cruelty' vs Leigh's 'moral centre': both are describing the same behaviour, which creates an immediate friction point—get them to argue about whether the label changes the thing itself

The veil passage (c16:p62): all three experts want to quote it but interpret it entirely differently—Trevelyan sees comedy sabotaging sentiment, Leigh sees moral interruption, Rosen sees systemic control over female desire. This is the segment's richest single moment

Rosen's structural reading vs Leigh's moral reading of ingratitude and resentment: Leigh says Hester's rebellion is spiritual failure; Rosen says it's rational response to colonized interiority—this should get heated

The c11:p49 'fly away like a cloud' quote: both Leigh and Rosen want to use it but for opposite purposes—Leigh reads it as revealing fantasy's moral shallowness, Rosen reads it as evidence of Catherine's totalizing grip on their inner lives

questions.question: Daniel, you said something in our chat that I keep coming back to — that the telegram isn't fate, it's capital moving through a wire. Oliphant writes it as this cosmic, breath-holding moment, Hester feeling the 'power of fate' suspended — but you're saying that's a con. Is Oliphant deceiving us, or is she deceiving herself?
questions.intent: Open the segment with Rosen's most provocative materialist reading of c27:p53 and immediately put pressure on whether this is a critique of Oliphant or a reading she'd endorse

questions.question: Oliver, you described the narrator's voice in that 'the fools!' passage — c37:p16 — as Oliphant *wading into* the story, not standing above it. But Edmund hears the same passage as austere moral authority, the novelist delivering judgment. Can you actually read that line aloud for us and tell me which one of you is hearing it right?
questions.intent: Get Trevelyan to perform the passage, reveal the tonal ambiguity, and directly set up disagreement with Leigh about whether it's fury or wisdom — also foregrounds the performative reading vs. classical reading divide

questions.question: Edmund, your whole reading rests on Hester being an active participant in her own undoing — she *knows* her casuistry will be 'partially seen through,' she chooses her own blindness. But Daniel would say that a young woman with no money and no power doesn't have the luxury of calling that a free choice. How do you answer that?
questions.intent: Force Leigh to defend his moral reading against Rosen's class reading — the sharpest disagreement in the room — using c21:p100 as the battleground

questions.question: Here's what I want to push on, Daniel — you say the house is the only character that doesn't suffer. But Oliver would argue that the house *performs* its own endurance, that even the house is trapped in a role. Is there a version of your reading where Oliphant is actually exposing that machinery rather than running cover for it?
questions.intent: Create space for Rosen and Trevelyan to find unexpected common ground while also clarifying whether the novel is conservative or critical — keeps the conversation from becoming a binary Leigh-vs-Rosen standoff

questions.question: Edmund, last question and I want a real answer — 'the house remains.' Is that Oliphant's consolation, or her verdict?
questions.intent: Close the segment with Leigh's strongest and most quotable formulation, but leave space for Rosen and Trevelyan to contest it — the phrase should resonate as an open question the audience takes away

briefs.steering_notes: The central fault line is Leigh's moral-classical reading versus Rosen's materialist reading, with Trevelyan playing a genuinely interesting middle position — he agrees with Leigh that the novel has moral authority but agrees with Rosen that the house is a trap. Don't let this collapse into two sides. Push Trevelyan to occupy his own ground rather than referee. The telegram passage (c27:p53) and the casuistry passage (c21:p100) should both get quoted aloud if possible — these are the two moments where all three readings diverge most sharply. Let Rosen be provocative early, then let Leigh answer hard, then let Trevelyan complicate both. End on the house image — it's the phrase that stays.
cross_engagement_targets: Rosen's reading of the telegram as capital-in-motion directly contradicts Leigh's reading of it as emotional and reputational stakes — both need to quote c27:p53 and argue over what Hester is actually perceiving

Trevelyan's claim that c21:p100 *performs* what it describes (the syntax mirrors the casuistry) is something Rosen would find useful but would reframe as class performance rather than aesthetic sophistication — this is a productive complement that could produce real cross-talk

Leigh's insistence that Hester *chooses* her blindness and Rosen's insistence that she has no real choice are the deepest disagreement in the room — the casuistry passage is the text they're both looking at and reading completely differently
Trevelyan and Rosen could converge unexpectedly on the house-as-performance reading, which would isolate Leigh's conservative-Burkean reading and give him something genuinely difficult to answer
